newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hyundai, Daewoo takeover of Kia seen possible.
newsitem.headline: Hyundai, Daewoo takeover of Kia seen possible.

text.p: Hours before creditors were to meet to map out bail-out details for the troubled Kia Group, analysts said on Wednesday that two of South Korea's biggest conglomerates had sent out feelers about a possible takeover.
Creditors were to meet later on Wednesday.

South Korea's leading newspaper Chosun Ilbo said on Wednesday the nation's largest carmaker Hyundai Motor and unlisted Daewoo were discussing a plan to jointly take over Kia and had agreed in principle to the deal.
The two automakers officially denied that such an agreement had been made, but some officials of the companies and analysts said the deal would be one of the most likely solutions to the Kia crisis.
The newspaper also said Daewoo Group chairman Kim Woo-choong and Hyundai Motor's honorary chairman Chung Se-yung had met last week to discuss the issue.

"We hope Kia will survive with its own self-rescue efforts. But Hyundai and Daewoo are now reviewing a joint takeover plan to prepare for a possible Kia failure," the newspaper quoted a senior Hyundai official as saying.
"A third party solution makes economic sense. That will please the financial community and political circles," said Kim Byung-joon, analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute.
Analysts said Kia's efforts to rescue itself were unlikely to succeed due to slumping domestic sales, tough competition in the world market and Kia's own managerial problems.

"In particular, creditors are worried about the security of their loans to Kia. They will welcome any overture by a big group with deep pockets that is interested in the ailing group," said a head researcher at a foreign securites house.
"A takeover deal will also ease concerns about serious over-capacity in South Korea's auto industry," he said.
But other analysts said a Hyundai takeover could be harmful to the auto sector as it would increase that company's dominance of the industry.

"A takeover would bring Hyundai's capacity to 2.5 million units and further strengthen its monopoly. If that happens, its economic benefit is very questionable," said Oh Kyu-chang, a researcher at the state-funded Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade (KIET).
Daewoo Motor might gain if it could buy Kia's commercial vehicle unit Asia Motors, which the Chosun Ilbo said was part of the deal.
"Asia Motors production lines will complete Daewoo's current line-up, which comprises passenger cars and commercial vehicles," said James Son, analyst at SBC Warburg Securities.
Ultimately, analysts said the Samsung Group was best candidate to take over Kia Motors.

"Samsung's takeover scenario looks like the best solution because it will most effectively ease concerns about serious over-capcity in South Korea's auto industry," said the analyst at the foreign securities house.

But labour unions and the management at the Kia Group have strongly opposed the Samsung takeover option because they believed Kia's problems were partly caused by Samsung's leaked report suggesting the restructuring of the car industry.
Samsung has no labour unions at any of its affiliates, while Kia's union are viewed as militant.
